So I commute to work by bicycle in one of the most bike-friendly cities in America, and have done so for years. When the weather is nice, I see hundreds of people going to their jobs, running errands, and even taking their kids to school via bike. During that same time, I've also seen people doing all sorts of bizarre activities on these same bikes: smoking, talking on a cell phone with no hands, playing a trumpet, jerking off, etc etc.

Today, though, I saw something brand new. As I was stopped at a long light, I took a look around and saw the usual assortment of fit, wiry folks from full on middle-aged freds to your stereotypical, way-cooler-than-me hipsters on fixies. At the way back of the pack, though, was something I wasn't used to seeing. A full on legbeard, complete with obesity and problem glasses, was riding up on a beach cruiser.

Now, seeing a tumblr stereotype outside in the sun wasn't what surprised me. What did make me stare, though, was this woman was fucking eating. Of all the weird things I've seen people doing in traffic, this was surprisingly unusual. She had a bag of candy in her front bike basket and had one hand that would normally be dedicated to controlling the handlebars or getting ready to brake dedicated instead to mainlining sugar. I couldn't stop from staring at her as she approached the group waiting at the light, and she caught me staring with what was no doubt a constrained look of disgust on my face.

A few blocks ahead, I was at another light with two travel lanes that requires everyone to make a left but allows right-hand turns from the right-most of the two lanes. Since it was two left-hand turn lanes turning onto a street with two lanes, I was at the far right of those two lanes so I could go directly to the bike lane on the other road as soon as the light turned. She came up beside me in the middle of the two left-turning lanes, and said "You know, you shouldn't be in that lane. People making a right are going to get stuck behind you when the light turns". I replied with a polite "I always wait here so I can get to the bike lane as fast as possible. I bike through this intersection a lot, don't worry about me."

What I wanted to say was "Just because you have trouble overcoming your massive inertia doesn't mean I have the same problem." As I sped away, I caught a glimpse of her wobbling awkwardly over to the bike lane while drivers behind her were presumably thinking "fucking cyclists, always clogging up the roads".

TL;DR: While biking home from work I see a fattie eating candy with one hand while biking through traffic. Later, she gives me shit advice on how to safely cross an intersection which I politely declined.

I know the title is kind of a "well, duh," but I found Unangst's comments about Microsoft's relationship with Steam to be pretty interesting:

"We are not intending to compete with Steam," he told me, "If anything, we want Steam to be even more successful—they've done great things for PC gamers in terms of having a single store.

"Over time do we want more developers to come over to our store and offer it in addition to Steam? Absolutely. Is competition good for people? Absolutely. But our goal right now isn't to do anything else other than support Steam and help it run great on Windows 10."

Valve has a pretty good handle on the PC gaming market, largely because Microsoft was so slow to capitalize on PC gaming and digital distribution. It'll be interesting if changing the formula allows them to make any kind of dent in Steam's marketshare.

Technically Steam is a 3rd party distribution channel. I think the difference is how invasive some of the distribution network is. Steam can be pretty hands-off, whereas Uplay and Origin tend to get in the way because they want you to see their networks as a value add. Like you said, sometimes the more valuable play is to just stay out of the way of your gaming.

I don't class steam as a 3rd party channel since its my main platform for games. It's as part of my PC as internet explorer or the task-bar at this point. Thats part of the problem for these companies, steam is so integrated into peoples lives that there's no way Origin or Uplay can compete and are just getting in the way.

Then I think it's more of a market leader problem and less of a 3rd party problem. Steam has such a big lead at this point that I don't think anyone can make a big dent in their market share. Even if you absolutely need Origin or Uplay for a handful of specific games, it's not going to get you off of Steam for the other 90% of your library. I think at this point the best Microsoft can hope for is either a victory by very slow and prolonged market growth, or for Valve to screw up pretty majorly and MS establishes itself as a solid alternative. In either case, Microsoft has its work cut out for it.

Edit: a third option would be to come in with a very strong value add that Valve can't quickly match, although I don't know what that might be. Maybe if they combined Xbox and PC in a way that allows you to play cross-platform against players on either system. It's something that Valve can't emulate quickly, and something that Microsoft is already touching on with Windows 10 and the upcoming Xbox One update.
They should give up on the whole gaming scene on PC and concentrate on integration.
